title: Obesity in Pediatric Patients -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Childhood obesity is one of the most prevalent chronic conditions in pediatric populations and has escalated into a global epidemic. Genetic, physiological, environmental, and socioeconomic factors contribute to the development of this condition. Childhood obesity increases the likelihood of adult obesity and places affected individuals at risk for serious short- and long-term adverse health outcomes and comorbidities. In the U.S., childhood obesity rates have more than tripled since the 1960s, with prevalence increasing with age.

title: Obesity in Pediatric Patients -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Diagnosis is based on body mass index percentiles adjusted for sex and age, along with evaluation for comorbidities such as dyslipidemia, hypertension, and insulin resistance. Management focuses on lifestyle modification through dietary changes, increased physical activity, and behavioral intervention. Pharmacologic and surgical therapies are reserved for severe cases with significant health risks. Delayed or inadequate prevention, diagnosis, and treatment contribute to pediatric comorbidities that frequently persist into adulthood.

title: Obesity in Pediatric Patients -- Introduction
content: Obesity is a complex and widespread health issue that often persists into adolescence. The prevalence of obesity in children aged 6 to 11 years increased from 4.2% between 1963 and 1965 to 15.3% between 1999 and 2000. According to the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey, approximately 20% of children in the U.S. have obesity, while another 16% have a body mass index (BMI) in the overweight category. title: Obesity in Pediatric Patients -- Introduction
content: Obesity is defined as having a BMI greater than or equal to the 95th percentile for age and sex in children 2 years and older. To minimize stigma and reflect current clinical practice, obesity is now categorized as class 1, 2, or 3 instead of being labeled "severe" or "morbid." Classes are defined based on percentiles of BMI for age  and sex from standardized growth charts, such as those from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) or the World Health Organization (WHO). Class 1 obesity: BMI greater than or equal to the 95th percentile but less than 120% of the 95th percentile Class 2 obesity: BMI greater than or equal to 120% but less than 140% of the 95th percentile Class 3 obesity: BMI greater than or equal to 140% of the 95th percentile. For children younger than 2 years, the CDC recommends using the WHO weight-for-length charts, which are age- and sex-specific, rather than the BMI. [2]

title: Obesity in Pediatric Patients -- Introduction
content: In 2025, a global commission on obesity, comprising representatives from various medical specialties and nations, proposed a comprehensive redefinition of obesity. The new criteria incorporate BMI along with at least 1 additional anthropometric measurement, such as waist circumference or waist-to-hip ratio, coupled with evidence of organ system dysfunction or functional limitations in activities of daily living. The commission classified children and adults with excess adiposity but no signs of organ dysfunction or functional impairment as having preclinical obesity, emphasizing the importance of early intervention to prevent significant health consequences. [3]

title: Obesity in Pediatric Patients -- Etiology
content: Obesity is a multifactorial condition, resulting from a complex interplay among genetic, biological, environmental, socioeconomic, and cultural drivers. Genetics and biology are predetermined, while other contributors may be modified. Modifiable factors include family behaviors related to eating, sleeping, and exercise, access to healthy food in schools and communities, availability of safe places for physical activity, and adverse childhood experiences.

title: Obesity in Pediatric Patients -- Etiology
content: Weight gain occurs when energy intake chronically exceeds energy expenditure, with both measured in calories, eventually leading to obesity. [5] Genetic determinants play a lesser role. Shifting food preferences in recent decades have been influenced by marketing and the increased availability of high-calorie, processed foods, such as fast food and sugar-sweetened beverages. The widespread consumption of hyperpalatable, energy-dense foods, combined with larger portion sizes and frequent snacking, has been strongly associated with the rising prevalence of obesity in industrialized nations. [6]

title: Obesity in Pediatric Patients -- Etiology
content: Feeding patterns are culturally influenced, with children often modeling their behavior after their parents and families from a young age. Research indicates that higher parental education and regular family meals have a positive influence on children's healthy food choices. Families eating together, exposing children to a variety of nutritious foods, and avoiding television during meals foster a positive food environment that reduces the likelihood of obesity. [9] The amount of time a child spends watching television and playing video games correlates with increased distracted eating and obesity. [10]

title: Obesity in Pediatric Patients -- Etiology
content: Other critical risk factors may predispose individuals to obesity. Perinatal and postnatal conditions that increase risk include elevated maternal BMI during pregnancy, large-for-gestational-age birth weight, rapid weight gain in infancy and early childhood, and the contrast between breastfeeding, a protective factor, and formula feeding. Environmental chemicals, microbiota, early antibiotic use, and adverse life experiences are also considered potential risk factors. [11] [12] [13]

title: Obesity in Pediatric Patients -- Etiology
content: Alterations in the gut microbiome may contribute to unhealthy weight gain, as dysbiosis increases the production of short-chain fatty acids associated with a higher risk of obesity, type 2 diabetes (T2D), and metabolic syndrome. [14] Prenatal exposure to endocrine-disrupting chemicals such as bisphenol A and dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane has been hypothesized to increase obesity risk by modulating estrogen receptor activity and altering metabolic programming. [15]

title: Obesity in Pediatric Patients -- Etiology
content: Polygenic and monogenic obesity, though uncommon, merit consideration. Polygenic obesity results from the interaction of several polygenic variants with environmental factors, increasing the likelihood of obesity. Further genetic and molecular studies are needed to determine the clinical significance of these genetic variations. Monogenic obesity is severe and has an early onset, typically caused by an autosomal recessive mutation in the leptin-melanocortin pathway. Deficiencies in melanocortin 4 receptors (MC4R) and proopiomelanocortin increase food-seeking behaviors in children, while leptin and leptin receptor deficiencies result in early-onset extreme obesity. [16]

title: Obesity in Pediatric Patients -- Etiology
content: Genetic disorders associated with obesity include Prader-Willi (PWS), Alstrom, Bardet-Biedl (BBS), and Beckwith-Wiedemann syndromes, as well as Albright hereditary osteodystrophy. [17] Secondary etiologies of obesity, such as endocrine, neurologic, psychological, and drug-induced causes, should be considered when the onset of obesity is sudden or unexpected. The resulting hormonal imbalances affecting satiety and food-seeking behaviors are the likely mechanisms promoting the condition in these cases.

title: Obesity in Pediatric Patients -- Epidemiology
content: Approximately 13.5 million American adolescents struggle with obesity. Disparities exist across racial and ethnic groups, with non-Hispanic Black and Mexican American children exhibiting higher rates of obesity than non-Hispanic White children. Factors such as parental educational level and income, access to healthy food options, and availability of safe physical activity opportunities contribute to disparities in obesity prevalence. Additionally, children with disabilities, including autism and intellectual disabilities, are at higher risk of developing obesity. [19]

title: Obesity in Pediatric Patients -- Pathophysiology
content: Appetite and satiety are controlled through neuroendocrine feedback mechanisms. Gastrointestinal hormones, such as ghrelin, stimulate appetite, while glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1), peptide YY (PYY), cholecystokinin, and vagal neural feedback inhibit appetite and promote satiety. [20]

title: Obesity in Pediatric Patients -- History and Physical
content: Evaluation of patients with obesity begins with a comprehensive medical history and a careful physical examination to identify the etiology and any comorbid conditions. This process typically occurs during a well-child visit at the medical home but may also take place during problem-focused appointments. The clinician should first inquire whether the family or patient has concerns about the child’s growth or weight. History-taking should begin with reviewing prenatal factors, such as maternal weight gain during pregnancy or gestational diabetes, which may increase the likelihood of obesity. Perinatal history should include questions about intrauterine growth retardation followed by rapid catch-up growth or whether the child was large for gestational age at birth.

title: Obesity in Pediatric Patients -- History and Physical
content: A nonjudgmental approach is essential when probing the details of a child’s nutritional intake and energy expenditure. Reviewing family feeding patterns, meal composition, snacking habits, and screen time can help uncover the cause of excessive weight gain. A 24-hour diet recall, which lists the servings of fruits, vegetables, and high-carbohydrate and high-calorie foods in meals, snacks, and beverages, provides valuable information. Additionally, noting the duration and type of physical activity can help assess energy expenditure.

title: Obesity in Pediatric Patients -- History and Physical
content: A family history of obesity and obesity-related comorbid conditions can provide further insights. Genetic susceptibility may be present, particularly if family members have experienced severe obesity requiring bariatric surgery, or the condition affects multiple generations. The presence of diabetes, hypertension, or cardiovascular disease in a family member increases the risk of a child developing similar conditions. Parental obesity is another risk factor, likely influenced by the interplay of genetics, shared environment, and social determinants of health. Clinicians should help families understand that childhood obesity increases the likelihood of developing several chronic diseases.

title: Obesity in Pediatric Patients -- History and Physical
content: Facial and body dysmorphisms may indicate underlying genetic disorders. For example, almond-shaped eyes, hypogonadism, and small hands and feet are characteristic of PWS. Other features, including hypotonia, upward-slanting eyes, a short neck, and transverse palmar creases, are associated with Down syndrome. A round face, central obesity, and excess fatty tissue on the upper back, particularly between the shoulders, may suggest Cushing syndrome. Cognitive impairment may also point to a genetic etiology. Short stature is commonly linked to hormone deficiencies and Albright hereditary osteodystrophy.

title: Obesity in Pediatric Patients -- Evaluation
content: Primary care clinicians typically diagnose obesity during health maintenance visits. The growth chart not only reveals the onset and severity of this condition but also provides clues about its potential causes. The BMI trajectory helps differentiate between a gradual increase during sensitive growth periods, such as infancy, childhood, and adolescence, and an abrupt acceleration. Sudden BMI changes may signal personal or family stress or medical issues such as tumors, trauma, hypothyroidism, and medication use.

title: Obesity in Pediatric Patients -- Evaluation
content: In children with obesity, evaluation for lipid abnormalities, prediabetes, T2D, and hepatic dysfunction should begin at age 10. Recommended assessments include a fasting lipid panel, fasting glucose, and alanine transaminase every 2 years. If fasting glucose is elevated, follow-up testing with hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) or a 2-hour plasma glucose level after an oral glucose tolerance test may be warranted.

title: Obesity in Pediatric Patients -- Treatment / Management -- Lifestyle and Behavioral Interventions
content: Evidence supports treating obesity and its comorbidities to achieve weight loss, prevent further weight gain, and improve related complications. Guidelines do not recommend a "watchful waiting" approach. Clinicians must document the presence of obesity and clearly explain to caregivers the importance of addressing this problem while avoiding stigmatizing the child. Asking for permission to discuss the child's BMI and weight can help facilitate this conversation. Labels like "obese child" must be avoided, and neutral terms, such as "unhealthy weight" or "gaining too much weight for age or height," must be used instead. The primary focus should remain on the child's health.

title: Obesity in Pediatric Patients -- Treatment / Management -- Lifestyle and Behavioral Interventions
content: Behavioral change is the cornerstone of managing pediatric obesity. Family-based interventions should center on reducing BMI by limiting the intake of sweetened beverages and fast food, increasing fruit and vegetable consumption, and promoting physical activity. Clinicians should provide clear recommendations on healthy food choices and portion sizes while also encouraging daily physical activity. Simply advising "eat less and exercise more" is too simplistic. Families should be encouraged to plan meals that take children's preferences into account while ensuring a balanced, nutrient-rich diet. [25]

title: Obesity in Pediatric Patients -- Treatment / Management -- Lifestyle and Behavioral Interventions
content: No single specific diet has been proven superior for weight loss. Approaches such as the "traffic light diet plan" can help families make healthy choices that respect cultural values and dietary practices. [26] Another commonly recommended strategy is the "5-2-1-0" guideline: 5 daily servings of fruits and vegetables, no more than 2 hours of screen time, at least 1 hour of physical activity, and 0 sugar-sweetened beverages. The American Heart Association advises limiting added sugars to no more than 25 g (6 tsp) per day and avoiding sugar-sweetened beverages altogether. [27]

title: Obesity in Pediatric Patients -- Treatment / Management -- Lifestyle and Behavioral Interventions
content: Creating a healthy food environment at home involves incorporating nutritious options for meals and snacks and avoiding screen time during meals. Children often model the behaviors of adults in the household, and positive family-level changes can significantly support both the prevention and treatment of obesity. [28] [29] Motivational interviewing can help assess the family's understanding of obesity-related health risks and guide them in adopting strategies that reflect their values and beliefs. [30] Involving both patients and their parents in goal-setting fosters sustainable and beneficial behavioral changes.

title: Obesity in Pediatric Patients -- Treatment / Management -- Lifestyle and Behavioral Interventions
content: The Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans recommend that children aged 6 to 17 years engage in at least 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity each day. Children aged 3 to 5 years should be physically active throughout the day to support growth and development. [31] Both aerobic and resistance exercises have been shown to improve the metabolic profile of children and reduce the risk of cardiovascular events. [32] Increasing physical activity can involve routines such as walking to school, participating in sports, engaging in unstructured outdoor play, and exercising with family members during leisure time. Encouraging family-wide physical activity is more effective in promoting a healthy, active lifestyle than focusing solely on the child. [33]

title: Obesity in Pediatric Patients -- Treatment / Management -- Lifestyle and Behavioral Interventions
content: Primary care clinicians, often working with limited resources and time, may find it challenging to provide the intensive behavior and lifestyle interventions recommended for obesity treatment. A structured weight management plan typically involves motivational interviewing and referrals to a registered dietitian or nutrition specialist. The next step often involves a comprehensive, multifaceted approach that includes more frequent and intensive behavior change sessions, typically delivered by an interprofessional team, with up to 22 sessions over a 3- to 12-month period. In some cases, patients may benefit from tertiary care interventions that include expert advice on nutrition and exercise, behavior counseling, pharmacologic therapy, and consideration of bariatric surgery.

title: Obesity in Pediatric Patients -- Treatment / Management -- Pharmacologic Treatment
content: Orlistat, approved by the FDA for use in children with obesity aged 12 years and older, is a pancreatic lipase inhibitor that promotes mild to moderate weight loss by inhibiting fat absorption. Although effective, the use of this drug may be limited by gastrointestinal adverse effects, including flatulence, fecal urgency, and steatorrhea. The recommended dose is 120 mg orally, 3 times daily. [34]

content: Metformin is FDA-approved for treating T2D in children aged 10 years and older. While not approved for weight loss, this medication has demonstrated mild-to-moderate weight reduction in pediatric patients receiving it for T2D. Metformin is also used in managing PCOS by decreasing hepatic glucose production, reducing intestinal glucose absorption, and enhancing insulin sensitivity. The starting dose is 500 mg orally, once or twice daily, and may be titrated to a maximum of 2,500 mg per day.

title: Obesity in Pediatric Patients -- Treatment / Management -- Surgery
content: Weight loss surgery can be a safe and effective option for pediatric patients with severe obesity. Candidates typically have a BMI of at least 35 kg/m² or 120% of the 95th percentile for age and sex, whichever is lower. The American Pediatric Surgical Association recommends surgical management for adolescents who have near-complete skeletal maturity and are at risk for medical complications related to obesity after failing intensive behavioral interventions in an interprofessional weight management program lasting at least 6 months. [36]

title: Obesity in Pediatric Patients -- Treatment / Management -- Surgery
content: Bariatric and metabolic surgeries, such as laparoscopic vertical sleeve gastrectomy and Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, are options for pediatric patients with severe obesity. Laparoscopic adjustable gastric band procedures are approved only for patients aged 18 years and older and are associated with lower long-term success and higher complication rates. Referral to comprehensive surgical centers with experience in caring for young patients and their families is recommended. Although no specific minimum age has been established, most bariatric procedures are performed in adolescents aged 13 years or older. Surgery may still be appropriate in selected cases involving younger children with severe comorbidities. Evaluation for bariatric surgery must consider chronological age, emotional maturity, and the patient’s capacity to adhere to necessary lifestyle changes. [37]

title: Obesity in Pediatric Patients -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Clinicians should evaluate for uncommon secondary causes and recognize medical conditions associated with obesity. Attenuated height growth velocity suggests endocrine causes like hypothyroidism, hypothalamic tumor, growth hormone deficiency, and Cushing syndrome. A history of significant head trauma requires ruling out central nervous system injury as the cause of hypothalamic obesity. In such cases, an abrupt change in the trajectory of weight gain is usually observed following the inciting event.

[38] MC4R deficiency is a cause of early-onset pediatric obesity and is diagnosed through molecular genetic studies.

Papilledema may be present on physical examination. Computed tomography and brain magnetic resonance imaging may be performed, but the definitive diagnostic test is the measurement of the cerebrospinal fluid opening pressure upon lumbar puncture. [39]

content: Early diagnosis and appropriate intervention lead to a decline in comorbidities and an improved overall prognosis. As the burden of complications increases with age and severity, timely diagnosis and treatment offer the best chance for good health. Clinicians must refer patients promptly for pharmacological and surgical interventions when lifestyle changes and behavioral interventions fail. Childhood obesity often persists into adulthood without appropriate treatment, increasing the risk of long-term adverse health outcomes.

title: Obesity in Pediatric Patients -- Complications
content: Treating pediatric obesity and its comorbid conditions is challenging, time-consuming, and often frustrating for both clinicians and families. Obesity impacts multiple organ systems, most notably the cardiovascular and endocrine systems. [41] Dyslipidemia, characterized by low high-density lipoprotein and high low-density lipoprotein and total cholesterol, as well as hypertension, increases the risk of future adverse cardiovascular events. Central adiposity, in particular, causes metabolic imbalances that lead to insulin resistance and metabolic syndrome, and it is commonly associated with PCOS. Excess adipose tissue can also interfere with the liver's metabolic and synthetic functions, contributing to the development of MASLD. Obesity is also associated with an increased risk of gallstones.

title: Obesity in Pediatric Patients -- Complications
content: The psychological complications of obesity can significantly impact a child's daily life and should be addressed early. Interviewing children nonjudgmentally with open-ended questions can encourage them to share any concerns they may have. Additionally, clinicians should inquire about symptoms of anxiety or depression, worsening grades, or experiences of bullying at school. Professional counseling may be necessary to prevent the progression of psychological symptoms.

content: Pediatric obesity is a complex problem that often requires an interprofessional team approach. Failure to adequately diagnose and treat this condition results in comorbid medical conditions and increases the likelihood of obesity in adulthood. The primary care clinician usually makes the initial diagnosis, but the subsequent management involves consultation with specialists in a staged manner. [43]

title: Obesity in Pediatric Patients -- Consultations
content: Stage 1, "Prevention Plus," involves recommendations from primary care clinicians. Children with a BMI between the 85th and 95th percentile are considered overweight. Nutritional advice should include increasing the intake of fruits and vegetables, reducing consumption of sugary drinks and fast foods, and maintaining regular, balanced meals. Clinicians should also assess screen time, sleep, and physical activity habits. Regular follow-up, typically within 3 to 6 months, is essential to monitor progress and make necessary adjustments.

title: Obesity in Pediatric Patients -- Consultations
content: Failure to improve in 3 to 6 months or a BMI in the obese range warrants consideration of Stage 2, structured weight management, which involves referral to a registered dietitian or nutrition specialist. Close follow-up is essential to monitor progress. For families experiencing food insecurity, referrals to community resources, such as the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), food pantries, and soup kitchens, should be provided.

title: Obesity in Pediatric Patients -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Family-based interventions have proven successful and sustainable in managing pediatric obesity. Educating families about healthy eating and exercise is a key factor in achieving positive outcomes. Families should be encouraged to prioritize healthy foods, minimize processed foods and high-calorie, sugary snacks, while increasing their intake of fruits and vegetables to at least 5 servings per day. The importance of creating a positive food environment should be emphasized.

title: Obesity in Pediatric Patients -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Healthy habits include eating breakfast daily, having regular family meals, and limiting meals and snacks outside the home. Parents should be discouraged from using food as a reward for their children. [44] Families should also engage in enjoyable physical activities tailored to the child's abilities. Involving caregivers in setting goals related to diet and exercise improves the effectiveness of these interventions. Caregivers can select food options that align with their cultural traditions and food preferences.

content: However, financial difficulties may lead parents to work multiple jobs to support their families, which can be an obstacle to family-based interventions. Food insecurity may force families to purchase higher-calorie, less nutritious foods. Unsupervised children are more likely to consume processed or fast foods, spend more time on screens, and engage in less physical activity. Additionally, some neighborhoods are unsafe for outdoor play and physical exercise. Clinicians must consider the child's home environment and any potential barriers to following medical recommendations to take a patient-centered approach to managing pediatric obesity. [45]

title: Obesity in Pediatric Patients -- Pearls and Other Issues
content: The 2025 Global Commission's guidelines may have unintended consequences for young people. Normative ranges for waist circumference or waist-to-hip ratio have not been validated for children, and the new criteria do not account for a child's growth or the role of BMI percentiles by age and sex. Patients currently identified as having obesity may no longer meet the criteria if they have yet to develop signs of organ dysfunction, which often do not appear until age 9 or older. Classifying these children as “preclinical” raises concern that payers may use this designation to deny necessary coverage for obesity-related care.

content: Obesity is a serious public health issue in the U.S. and other countries, with a concerning increase in prevalence over the past few decades. Primary obesity arises from an imbalance between energy intake and expenditure. Secondary causes, such as endocrine problems, genetic conditions, and head trauma, are less common but must be ruled out before prescribing treatment.

title: Obesity in Pediatric Patients -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Primary care clinicians typically diagnose obesity using the patient’s history, physical examination, and growth chart review. However, comprehensive management requires collaboration with an interprofessional team that may include nurses, dietitians, nutrition specialists, psychologists, behavioral counselors, exercise specialists, endocrinologists, neurologists, podiatrists, and surgeons. Nurses and nurse practitioners play a crucial role, especially in pediatric primary care, by educating and motivating families and children to adopt healthier habits.
